comparator.sourceNotes: The programme pages (s1, s2, s3) describe the structure only in words: an academic core, two to four general education courses, a concentration in the social sciences, humanities or sciences (or an interdisciplinary mix), skills trainings, three-week projects and a Capstone. They give no EC, and the 'View current courses' catalogue is not readable from this environment (the 2024-2025 curriculum PDF is blank). The 180-EC reconstruction therefore follows the 2026-2027 Education and Examination Regulations of the Maastricht School of Liberal Arts and Sciences (s0, UCM programme; in force 1 September 2026): Article 3.6 (180 EC), 3.7 (components), 3.8 (core of four 5-EC courses plus core skills trainings and projects of 20 EC for UCM, and 10-20 EC of general education), 3.9 (concentration of 14-16 courses and 70-80 EC, six skills trainings of 15 EC, three projects of 15 EC, and a 20-EC Capstone) and Appendix I (named core courses COR1002, COR1003, COR1004, COR1007; core skills trainings SKI1008, SKI1004, SKI1005; core projects PRO1014 of 7.5 EC and PRO1012 of 5 EC). The regulations do not state the credit value of each core skills training; 2.5 EC each follows from the 20-EC core skills-and-projects total (20 minus 7.5 and 5 leaves 7.5 EC for three skills trainings) and from the 2.5 EC per skills training in Article 3.9(4). Fixed components total 90 EC (core courses 20, core skills and projects 20, concentration skills 15, projects 15, Capstone 20); the remaining 90 EC are general education plus concentration courses, where the regulations allow 10-20 and 70-80 EC. I instantiated the midpoint (3 general education courses, 15 EC; 15 concentration courses, 75 EC), which is valid. The concentration domain, its courses, the general education courses and the choice of skills trainings and projects are individual student choices that the official sources do not fix, so they are kept as explicit restricted-choice components without invented course names. Article 3.9(11) also permits an interdisciplinary concentration, which does not change the 180-EC structure. Checked 2026-10-02. A human may wish to confirm the core skills-training credits and the 15/75 split against the UCM course catalogue.

alternatives.concept: UCM has no single curriculum: every student takes the same academic core (philosophy of science, political philosophy, contemporary world history, liberal arts education), research methods, general education outside the chosen domain, a concentration with skills trainings and projects, and a Capstone, and the programme's own pages present combining the social sciences, humanities and natural sciences as its defining idea. The strongest defensible UCR response reproduces that structure as an interdisciplinary programme: UCR counterparts of the academic core in philosophy, history and political thought, research methods and statistics, a social-science and humanities concentration built from the political science, international relations, law, conflict, public policy and sociology directions that UCM lists, a documentary project, and natural-science and data courses as the general-education domain.

alternatives.labelRationale: The completed curriculum has seven political science, international relations and law courses (Foundations of Comparative Politics, Theory of International Relations, Peace & Conflict, European Union Politics, Law Society & Justice, Human Rights, Public International Law), four sociology courses, four philosophy and history courses forming the academic-core counterpart (Introduction to Western Philosophy, Modern History, Introduction to Political Philosophy, Ethics) plus two further history courses, three research-methods and data courses, two sustainability courses, one documentary-media course and Personal & Professional Development. It is therefore an interdisciplinary social-science and humanities programme with methods and sustainability, and not a single-field programme.

alternatives.concept: UCM lists psychology, cognitive science and neuroscience, biomedical science and global health as stable study directions, and its sciences domain lets a student build a concentration around them. This alternative takes that direction as its organising logic instead of the interdisciplinary social-science and humanities core: a programme on how the brain, behaviour and the body produce health and illness, moving from the brain-and-behaviour and life-and-health gateways to psychology, cognitive neuroscience, physiology, pathology and public health, and ending with advanced seminars and a systematic-review methods course.

alternatives.labelRationale: The completed curriculum has eight psychology courses (Social Psychology, Statistics & Experimental Methods, Abnormal Psychology, Lifespan Developmental Psychology, Medical & Health Psychology, Advanced Research Seminar, Youth Resilience to Extremism, Psychodiagnostics & Psychotherapies), five cognitive science and neuroscience courses (including Philosophy of Mind), eight biomedical and life science courses, one public health course, the brain-and-behaviour gateway and Personal & Professional Development. It is therefore a sciences-domain programme on mind, brain and health spanning psychology, neuroscience and biomedicine, not a psychology-only or biomedicine-only programme.
alternatives.distinctnessRationale: Alternative 1 is organised around the UCM academic core and a social-science and humanities concentration in politics, international relations, law and sociology, and has no psychology, neuroscience or biomedical course. Alternative 2 is organised around the sciences domain and psychology: it keeps only Personal & Professional Development and Statistics & Experimental Methods from Alternative 1 and replaces 22 of 24 courses with psychology, cognitive science, neuroscience, biomedical science and public health courses. The two programmes share 2 courses and each differs from the other by 22 courses (165 EC), well above the 30 EC / 4-course floor, and the differing courses follow directly from the change of organising direction, not from substitutions.

alternatives.concept: UCM's humanities domain lists arts and literature, cultural studies, media studies, history and philosophy, and its projects include research-based documentaries. This alternative builds a humanities concentration around the arts and literature, cultural studies and media studies directions: how stories, images, films, media and public rhetoric produce and contest meaning in different cultures, supported by philosophy, history of gender, qualitative research methods and a documentary course.

progressionAssessment.rationale: Every formal prerequisite is scheduled in an earlier semester: Law, Society & Justice (semester 3) precedes Introduction to Public International Law (semester 4). Advisory progression is respected: the introductory philosophy, history, political philosophy and law courses are in semester 1, Introduction to Sociology and Modern Sociology (semester 3) precede New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory (semester 5), which builds on both, and the methods courses Research Methods & Statistics (semester 2) and Qualitative Research Methodology (semester 4) precede the research-oriented History Research Seminar and the other 300-level courses of semesters 5 and 6. Personal & Professional Development is in semester 2 of Year 1, because its availability and the 4-courses-per-semester pattern leave no room for it in semester 1.

alternativeSelection.assessment: Three UCR alternatives are defensible and the maximum was reached. UCM has no single curriculum: it is an interdisciplinary college whose students choose one of three domains, so the closest response (Alternative 1) is an interdisciplinary programme that reproduces the fixed UCM structure (academic core counterparts, research methods, general-education sciences and a social-science and humanities concentration). It owns fifteen generator-eligible rows: 6062 and 6063 (combining social sciences, humanities and natural sciences; investigating problems from different perspectives), 6064 to 6066 (social-science, humanities and natural-science research), 6068, 6071, 6072, 6073, 6075 and 6076 (conflict studies, international law, international relations, political science, public policy, sociology), 6077 (statistics and quantitative analysis), 6080 and 6082 (history, philosophy) and 6088 (sustainability and climate change), each implemented by courses in Alternative 1. Alternative 2 is built on the four sciences-domain and psychology directions 6074, 6083, 6084 and 6085 and Alternative 3 on the humanities directions 6078, 6079 and 6081; each shares at most 5 courses with another alternative (Alternative 1 and 2 share 2, Alternative 1 and 3 share 5, Alternative 2 and 3 share 1) and differs by at least 19 courses, so all pairs pass the 30 EC / 4-course floor. The remaining generator-eligible directions, business administration, economics and international development (6067, 6069, 6070) and information and computer science and mathematics (6086, 6087), are coherent and feasible candidates but were not needed once three alternatives were included: maximum-reached. Search-only outcome rows (6098 to 6110) and support-only curricular topics (6089 to 6097) did not generate any alternative.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both address twentieth-century and recent world history; Modern History surveys 1815 to 2025 including the world wars, the Cold War and decolonisation, over a longer period than the past 75 years that Contemporary World History covers.

Both study political philosophy; Introduction to Political Philosophy examines influential Western thinkers on human nature, society and political authority and tests their theories against present problems, which is the subject of Political Philosophy in the UCM core.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Philosophy of Science treats the epistemology of scientific inquiry; UCR has no philosophy-of-science course, and Introduction to Western Philosophy (which covers the nature of knowledge among many other themes) was not judged a direct counterpart.

Both develop core academic skills; Personal & Professional Development trains selecting and critically analysing sources, articulating research questions and arguments and academic writing, which is the educational function of an introduction to academic skills, although UCM's component is a 2.5-EC skills training.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Liberal Arts and Science Education in the 21st Century reflects on the nature of liberal arts education; Personal & Professional Development concerns personal formation and academic skills and is matched to the academic-skills component instead.

Both are introductions to research methods; Research Methods & Statistics covers research design, operationalisation, sampling and descriptive and inferential statistics, which is an important and identifiable part of introductory research-methods training, although UCM's skills training content is not published.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Research Methods II is a 2.5-EC skills training whose content is not published on a readable page; no UCR course was judged a specific counterpart beyond the introductory methods course already matched.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Introduction to Academic Skills II is a 7.5-EC first-year project; UCR has no corresponding project course in the scheduled curriculum.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the Research Project is a 5-EC first-year project; no scheduled UCR course is a project of that kind.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the six concentration skills trainings are individual choices (for example interviewing and systematic reviews) that the sources do not name, so no UCR course can be matched to them as a group.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the three concentration projects are individual choices of three-week projects, internships or research projects that the sources do not name, so no UCR course can be matched to them as a group.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: general education is an individual restricted choice of three courses outside the concentration domain that the sources do not name; the UCR programmes spread their courses across domains differently and no single course corresponds to it.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the fifteen concentration courses depend on the domain the student chooses and are not named in the sources; the UCR concentration-like course groups appear in the blocks above without being forced onto this open component.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the 20-EC Capstone is an individual advanced research or analytical project; UCR has no scheduled Capstone course, and the standardized optional independent research element is shown against this component.

notes.text: University College Maastricht organizes study around a fixed academic core, general education, a concentration chosen in the social sciences, humanities or sciences (or an interdisciplinary mix), skills trainings, projects and a Capstone. At UCR, comparable subjects are distributed across courses in political science, law, sociology, philosophy, history, psychology, neuroscience, biomedical science, literature and media. The UCR programmes therefore cover related territory through a different curricular structure rather than reproducing the UCM programme component by component, and each UCR alternative stands for one possible concentration route.

Both programmes include substantial study of philosophy, history, political thought and research methods in the first years. The UCM core additionally includes Philosophy of Science, Liberal Arts and Science Education in the 21st Century, project modules and a 20-EC Capstone. UCR students can instead combine courses from the Government & Society, Health, Cognition & Behavior and Media, Culture & Communication clusters, but those components are not offered as separate courses.
